H.fun_fact: The hydrogen in a glass of water is over 13 billion years old.

He.fun_fact: Helium leaks through rubber balloons because its atoms are smaller than rubber's polymer gaps.

Li.fun_fact: A lithium-ion phone battery contains enough lithium to make about 12 AA batteries.

Be.fun_fact: Beryllium is so stiff that a beryllium golf club can ping 17% farther than steel.

B.fun_fact: The boric acid in roach-killing powder is the same chemical used in eyewash solution — concentration is everything.

C.fun_fact: The carbon in your body has been recycled through stars, dinosaurs, and other humans over billions of years.

N.fun_fact: The nitrogen in fertilizers grown in Iowa could have come from Chilean saltpeter mined in the 1800s.

O.fun_fact: Breathing 100% oxygen for too long is toxic — the same molecule that sustains life damages lungs at high concentrations.

F.fun_fact: Fluorine is so reactive it burns through glass — it's stored in special containers and handled with extreme care.

Ne.fun_fact: The red glow in a neon sign is actually neon — other colors like blue and green come from different gases.

Na.fun_fact: Sodium explodes when it touches water — yet combined with chlorine it becomes the salt on your food.

Mg.fun_fact: Magnesium burns so brightly it's used in flares and was once used in camera flashbulbs.

Al.fun_fact: Aluminum was once more valuable than gold — Napoleon served honored guests on aluminum plates.

Si.fun_fact: The entire internet runs on silicon chips made from ordinary beach sand.

P.fun_fact: Phosphorus in matches was discovered by an alchemist trying to make gold from urine — both glow in the dark.

S.fun_fact: Sulfur gave volcanoes their 'hellfire' reputation — the Bible's brimstone is sulfur.

Cl.fun_fact: Chlorine was first used as a chemical weapon in WWI — today it's used to make your drinking water safe.

Ar.fun_fact: Argon in light bulbs prevents the tungsten filament from evaporating, extending bulb life.

K.fun_fact: A banana contains enough potassium-40 (a radioactive isotope) to trigger airport radiation detectors.

Ca.fun_fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza is made almost entirely of calcium carbonate — 2.3 million blocks of limestone.

Sc.fun_fact: Scandium is so rare that most people will never own an object containing it.

Ti.fun_fact: Titanium is used in sunscreen as TiO₂ — the white stuff that makes it opaque.

V.fun_fact: The Eiffel Tower's iron alloy contains vanadium, which is why it has withstood winds for over 130 years.

Cr.fun_fact: Chromium makes stainless steel stainless by forming an invisible self-repairing oxide layer.

Mn.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians added manganese to glass to make it colorless — the same glass-making trick still used today.

Fe.fun_fact: There's enough iron in your blood to make a nail about 3 cm long.

Co.fun_fact: Cobalt blue has been used by Chinese potters for 1,000 years; the same pigment colors blue Wedgwood pottery.

Ni.fun_fact: The US nickel coin is 75% copper and only 25% nickel — the penny is 97.5% zinc with just a copper coating.

Cu.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians used copper compounds as makeup — they didn't know it also killed eye bacteria.

Zn.fun_fact: Every penny minted after 1982 is a zinc coin with a thin copper coating — not a copper coin.

Ga.fun_fact: Gallium melts in your hand at 29.8°C — just above room temperature. You can pour it like mercury but it's non-toxic.

Ge.fun_fact: Germanium was predicted by Mendeleev in 1871 as 'eka-silicon' before it was discovered in 1886 — a triumph of the periodic table.

As.fun_fact: Victorian green wallpaper pigment contained arsenic — Napoleon may have been slowly poisoned by his damp wallpapered room.

Se.fun_fact: Selenium in dandruff shampoo kills the yeast that causes flaking — the same element is essential for your thyroid.

Br.fun_fact: Most flame retardants in sofas and mattresses contain bromine — your living room furniture is laced with it.

Kr.fun_fact: Krypton was used to define the meter from 1960–1983 — one meter was exactly 1,650,763.73 krypton wavelengths.

Rb.fun_fact: Rubidium clocks lose only one second every 300 years — your phone's time is ultimately synced to one.

Sr.fun_fact: Every red firework contains strontium — without it, fireworks would have no red color at all.

items: Yttrium iron garnets in microwave filters
Y.fun_fact: The yttrium phosphor in LED lights is what converts blue light to white — it's in every LED bulb you own.

Zr.fun_fact: Cubic zirconia (ZrO₂) is virtually indistinguishable from diamond to the naked eye — and costs 1% as much.

Nb.fun_fact: Almost all niobium production goes into making special steel — the steel in your car likely contains niobium.

Mo.fun_fact: Molybdenum disulfide is a lubricant so slippery it's used in spacecraft components and gun barrels.

items: No household uses — radioactive and synthetic
Tc.fun_fact: Technetium was the first element to be artificially created (1937). Every atom on Earth was made in a lab.

Ru.fun_fact: The hard drive in your computer likely has a single atomic layer of ruthenium that stores ten times more data.

Rh.fun_fact: Rhodium in catalytic converters converts toxic car exhaust into harmless nitrogen, CO₂, and water.

Pd.fun_fact: Palladium is rarer than platinum, and since 2019 has been more expensive — demand from catalytic converters drove the price up.

Ag.fun_fact: Silver is the most electrically conductive element — every copper wire connection in your home could theoretically be replaced by silver.

Cd.fun_fact: Nickel-cadmium batteries (NiCd) powered most cordless tools before lithium-ion took over. Cadmium is toxic — disposal matters.

In.fun_fact: The transparent coating on your phone screen is indium tin oxide — every touchscreen depends on this rare element.

Sn.fun_fact: Tin cans are mostly steel — only a thin tin coating prevents rusting. It's thinner than a human hair.

Sb.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians ground antimony sulfide to make the black kohl eyeliner seen on mummies.

Te.fun_fact: Your Blu-ray disc uses tellurium to store data: a laser melts and re-freezes a tiny telluride film to encode 1s and 0s.

I.fun_fact: Iodine was added to salt in 1924 after goiter (caused by iodine deficiency) affected 40% of Americans in some regions.

items: Bright flashlights and camera flash (xenon arc)
Xe.fun_fact: Xenon is the only noble gas used as a general anesthetic — it's expensive but leaves the body completely unchanged.

Cs.fun_fact: The official definition of one second is exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of cesium-133 — your phone's clock traces back to this.

Ba.fun_fact: Drinking a thick barium sulfate milkshake before an X-ray lets doctors see your digestive system in white — it's completely non-toxic.

La.fun_fact: The flint in a cigarette lighter is a mischmetal — a mix of rare earth elements including lanthanum.

Ce.fun_fact: The scratchy black coating inside self-cleaning ovens is cerium oxide — it catalyzes food into ash at high temperature.

Pr.fun_fact: Praseodymium in welders' goggles absorbs infrared radiation — the same rare earth that makes your hard drive motor spin.

items: Strong magnets in headphones, hard drives, motors
Nd.fun_fact: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets known — one the size of a coin can lift 300 times its own weight.

items: No household uses — radioactive and synthetic
Pm.fun_fact: Promethium has no stable isotopes. Every atom on Earth was either made in a reactor or decayed long ago.

items: Samarium cobalt magnets in some headphones
Sm.fun_fact: Samarium-cobalt magnets were the strongest available before neodymium magnets were invented in the 1980s.

items: Euro banknote security ink (glows red under UV)
Red phosphor in old CRT TVs
Eu.fun_fact: The red glow when you hold a euro note under UV light comes from europium — it's the anti-counterfeiting element.

Gd.fun_fact: Gadolinium is injected into patients before MRI scans — its strong magnetic properties make soft tissues visible.

items: Green phosphor in energy-saving light bulbs
Tb.fun_fact: The bright green color in LED and fluorescent lights often comes from terbium phosphors.

items: Neodymium magnets (dysprosium additive for heat resistance)
Dy.fun_fact: Electric car motors need dysprosium added to their magnets so they don't demagnetize when the motor heats up.

Ho.fun_fact: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any element — but it must be cooled near absolute zero to use this property.

Er.fun_fact: Long-distance fiber optic cables use erbium amplifiers every 100 km to boost the signal without converting to electricity.

Tm.fun_fact: Thulium-170 can replace bulky X-ray machines in the field — a tiny radioactive thulium source fits in a briefcase.

Yb.fun_fact: Ytterbium optical clocks are so accurate they'd lose only one second every 10 billion years — outlasting Earth's lifespan.

Lu.fun_fact: Lutetium crystals in PET scanners convert gamma rays to visible light to map cancer in your body.

items: Computer processor chips (hafnium oxide gate dielectric)
Hf.fun_fact: Modern Intel and AMD chips use hafnium oxide as a gate insulator — it replaced silicon oxide to prevent leakage in tiny transistors.

Ta.fun_fact: Your smartphone contains about 40 mg of tantalum in its capacitors — nearly every phone on Earth needs it.

W.fun_fact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals (3,422°C) — it's why light bulb filaments survived billions of on-off cycles.

Re.fun_fact: Single-crystal rhenium superalloy turbine blades in jet engines operate above their own melting point using cooling holes.

Os.fun_fact: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element — a cube the size of a baseball would weigh over 5 kg.

Ir.fun_fact: The iridium tip on your fountain pen nib is harder than sapphire — and virtually immune to corrosion.

Pt.fun_fact: Cisplatin, the most widely used cancer chemotherapy drug, is a simple platinum compound discovered by accident in 1965.

Au.fun_fact: All the gold ever mined in human history would fit in a cube about 21 meters on a side — barely the size of a large house.

Hg.fun_fact: Compact fluorescent bulbs (CFLs) contain mercury vapor — breaking one requires ventilation and careful cleanup.

items: Old rat poison (thallium sulfate, now banned)
Tl.fun_fact: Thallium was banned as rat poison because it's colorless, tasteless, and odorless — making it tragically easy to misuse.

Pb.fun_fact: Roman plumbers used lead pipes — the word 'plumber' comes from plumbum, the Latin word for lead.

Bi.fun_fact: Pepto-Bismol's active ingredient is bismuth — a heavy metal that's surprisingly gentle on upset stomachs.

Po.fun_fact: Polonium-210 in anti-static brushes used in darkrooms ionizes air to neutralize static on film — it's completely sealed.

items: No household uses — extremely rare radioactive
At.fun_fact: Astatine is so rare that the total amount ever isolated by humanity would be invisible to the naked eye.

items: Radon gas in basements (natural occurrence, hazard)
Rn.fun_fact: Radon seeps from granite rock into basements and is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

Fr.fun_fact: Francium is the most unstable naturally occurring element — its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only 22 minutes.

items: Old watch dials (radium paint, now banned)
Ra.fun_fact: Radium-painted watch dials from the 1920s still glow and are still radioactive — some are dangerous to own.

Ac.fun_fact: Actinium-225 is being studied for targeted cancer therapy — it can kill individual tumor cells without harming neighbors.

Th.fun_fact: Old camping lantern mantles contained thorium-232, a mildly radioactive material — modern ones use yttrium instead.

items: No household uses — rare and radioactive
Pa.fun_fact: The entire global supply of protactinium ever isolated would fit in a teaspoon.

U.fun_fact: Vaseline glass (yellow-green Depression-era glassware) glows bright green under UV — it's colored with uranium oxide.

Np.fun_fact: Neptunium was the first synthetic transuranium element, discovered in 1940 by bombarding uranium with neutrons.

Pu.fun_fact: Plutonium-238 powered the Voyager 1 probe, which is now in interstellar space — the farthest human-made object ever.

Am.fun_fact: Every ionization smoke detector in your home contains about 1 microgram of Americium-241 — enough to sense smoke particles.

items: Alpha particle sources in space instruments
Cm.fun_fact: Curium powered the alpha proton X-ray spectrometer on the Mars rovers, identifying elements in Martian rocks.

Bk.fun_fact: Only a few grams of berkelium have ever been made. It was first synthesized at the University of California, Berkeley.

items: Portable neutron sources for oil well logging
Cf.fun_fact: Californium-252 is the most expensive material ever sold commercially — it was once priced at $27 million per gram.

Es.fun_fact: Einsteinium was discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952 — it was classified for years.

Fm.fun_fact: Fermium was also discovered in H-bomb debris. Less than a microgram has ever been produced.

Md.fun_fact: Mendelevium was named for the creator of the periodic table. Only atoms-at-a-time have ever been made.

No.fun_fact: Nobelium was named after Alfred Nobel. Its most stable isotope lasts just 58 minutes.

Lr.fun_fact: Lawrencium completes the actinide series. It was first made in 1961 at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Rf.fun_fact: Rutherfordium atoms last only about 65 seconds — just long enough to confirm their existence.

Db.fun_fact: Dubnium was the subject of a Cold War naming dispute between American and Soviet labs — both claimed its discovery.

Sg.fun_fact: Seaborgium was named for Glenn Seaborg while he was still alive — one of the few elements named for a living person.

Bh.fun_fact: Bohrium's most stable isotope lasts about 61 seconds.

Hs.fun_fact: Hassium was first synthesized in 1984 at the GSI laboratory in Germany. Only a few dozen atoms exist at any time.

Mt.fun_fact: Meitnerium was named for Lise Meitner, co-discoverer of nuclear fission — one of the greatest scientists never to win a Nobel Prize.

Ds.fun_fact: Darmstadtium was first made by smashing nickel atoms into lead. Its longest-lived isotope lasts about 10 seconds.

Rg.fun_fact: Roentgenium was named for Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays. It decays in under 30 seconds.

Cn.fun_fact: Copernicium is predicted to be a gas at room temperature — extraordinary for a metal-row element.

Nh.fun_fact: Nihonium (element 113) was discovered by a Japanese team in 2004 — the first element found in Asia.

Fl.fun_fact: Flerovium may behave more like a noble gas than a metal — theory suggests its electrons relativistically contract.

Mc.fun_fact: Moscovium was synthesized in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia.

Lv.fun_fact: Livermorium was jointly discovered by Russian and American teams during a period of scientific cooperation in the early 2000s.

Ts.fun_fact: Tennessine, element 117, was first synthesized in 2010 using berkelium targets made at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

Og.fun_fact: Oganesson is the heaviest confirmed element. Its few atoms last less than a millisecond, then vanish.
